The recorded answer still has `exit_ok` false, `aborted` true, `StandardError`, and exactly one event -- `["reverting", ...]` with no matching `["reverted", ...]`.  Only the class name in that one event moves. (1) The requirement's own migration: db/migrate/20160119120000_widen_subscribers_email.rb, `class WidenSubscribersEmail < ActiveRecord::Migration[7.0]` with a single `change_column :subscribers, :email, :text`.  It is the 44th file under db/migrate/ and the highest-numbered, so every reading of `db:migrate`, `db:migrate:status` and `db:version` sees it.  Measured on the golden: /tmp/step07-golden/logs/verifier/observed.json, world `migrate`.
(2) activerecord-7.0.10 lib/active_record/migration.rb:1063-1073 `format_arguments`, which now does `last_arg.reject { |k, _v| internal_option?(k) }`, and :1075-1077 `internal_option?(name) = name.start_with?("_")`.  Neither method body carries that filter in activerecord-6.1.7.10.  The option is still set, at activerecord-7.0.10 lib/active_record/migration/compatibility.rb:114-121 (`V6_0#add_reference`), and still read, at activerecord-7.0.10 lib/active_record/connection_adapters/abstract/schema_definitions.rb:207.
(3) activerecord-7.0.10 lib/active_record/migration/compatibility.rb:35-57: `class V6_1 < V7_0`, `PostgreSQLCompat.compatible_timestamp_type` ("For Rails <= 6.1, :datetime was aliased to :timestamp ... From Rails 7 onwards, you can define what :datetime resolves to") and `V6_1#add_column`, which sets `options[:precision] ||= nil` and rewrites the type.  The whole `V6_1` class is new in 7.0.  These migrations declare `[4.2]`, and `V4_2 < V5_0 < V5_1 < V5_2 < V6_0 < V6_1`, so they inherit it.  The PostgreSQL side is activerecord-7.0.10 CHANGELOG.md:2268, "PostgreSQL: introduce `ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::PostgreSQLAdapter.datetime_type`".
migrate/migrate.up.why:
Three changes in one case, and only the first of them is this step's doing.

(1) The step's requirement adds a migration, so `db:migrate` runs one more of them: the recorded event list grows from 139 entries to 142, the three being `["migrating", "WidenSubscribersEmail"]`, `["op", "change_column(:subscribers, :email, :text)"]` and `["migrated", "WidenSubscribersEmail"]`, appended after the 43 the repository shipped.  Nothing earlier in the list moves, because the new file sorts last.

(2) `add_reference(:questions, :voice_file, ...)` stops naming `:_uses_legacy_reference_index_name=>true` in its log line.  The option is still set -- Rails 7.0's `V6_0#add_reference` sets it exactly as 6.1's did -- and the index the migration builds is therefore the same index.  What changed is the logging: 7.0's `format_arguments` drops every option whose name begins with an underscore, on the reasoning that an option the framework passes to itself is not part of what the migration was asked to do.  A reader of the log sees less; the database sees the same thing.

(3) `add_column(:subjects, :most_recent_activity, :datetime)` and `add_column(:notification_subscriptions, :last_email_sent_at, :datetime)` are logged as `:timestamp` with `{:precision=>nil}`.  Rails 7.0 gave `datetime` columns a default precision and made what `:datetime` resolves to configurable on PostgreSQL, so migrations written for 6.1 and earlier are routed through a compatibility shim that asks for the old type by its old name and pins the precision back to none.  The proof that the column is unchanged is in the tree rather than in the argument: `db/schema.rb` dumped from the step 06 golden and from the step 07 golden differ in the header, the version line and the `subscribers.email` type this step widens -- and in nothing else.  `most_recent_activity` and `last_email_sent_at` are byte-identical in the two dumps.

subscriptions/notify.new_activity_mail.why: A consequence of `sub.case_variant`, two scenario steps later.  The weekly digest lists every location its recipient subscribes to, so resident@example.com's mail now carries one more heading: `["h1", "Stork Club View"]`, inserted between Beer Revolution and Eli's Mile High Club, with no `Opinions -`/`Messages -` headings under it because nothing has been said about that location.  The recipient, the subject, the number of messages and every other heading are unchanged, and the `<TS:0>` timestamps are still normalised away.  Nothing about Action Mailer or the digest changed at this rung; the subscriber has one more subscription than they used to, for the reason given on subscriptions/sub.case_variant.

subscriptions/sub.case_variant.why:
This case posts RESIDENT@example.com -- an existing subscriber's address in capitals -- for a third location, and it is the visible half of what the step is asking for.

Before this step the controller's `find_or_create_by!` issued a literal `WHERE email = 'RESIDENT@example.com'`, PostgreSQL compared it case-sensitively, no row matched, and so it tried to create a second subscriber.  `validates :email, uniqueness: { case_sensitive: false }` then refused it, `find_or_create_by!` raised `ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid`, and the recorded answer was Rails's 422 page: "The change you wanted was rejected."  That is the recording from step 01 through step 06 -- an existing subscriber who typed their own address in capitals could not subscribe to another location.

From this step the column is encrypted deterministically with `downcase: true`, so the address is folded to lower case before the ciphertext is computed, on the way into the row and on the way into the lookup alike.  The lookup therefore finds the row that is already there, nothing is created, no validation is reached, and the subscription to location 3 is made like any other: 200, `body_class` "subscription create", "You just subscribed to receive notifications for: Stork Club".

The case-insensitive identity the 422 was enforcing has not been dropped -- it has moved one layer earlier, from a validation that compares two rows to a normalisation that gives the same address one representation.  That is exactly what this step gates, twice over, in `email_case_identity_kept` and `email_no_duplicate_row`, and those two gates are where the property is measured; this case records what a caller sees when it holds.  The adversarial reading survives the flip: a tree that encrypts without folding the case answers 200 here too, and is caught by the gates rather than by the recording, while a tree that drops encryption altogether fails five gates before this case is reached.

subscriptions/sub.case_variant_mail.why: A consequence of `sub.case_variant` and recorded separately because the mailbox is a separate observation: the subscription now succeeds, so the confirmation mail the `SubscriptionConfirmer` sends for every new location subscription goes out, and the case goes from an empty mailbox to one message.  The envelope is worth reading -- `to` and `envelope_to` are resident@example.com, the folded form, for a request that was made in capitals -- and the body names Stork Club, the third location, with a freshly minted confirmation token.  Before this step the 422 meant no LocationSubscription and therefore no mail.

subscriptions/unsub.tokens_seen.why: A count, and it counts the confirmation tokens the application minted over the whole scenario.  `sub.case_variant` now produces a subscription and therefore a fourth confirmation mail carrying a fifth token, so the number goes from 4 to 5.  The case is recorded rather than branched on precisely so that a change in how many tokens the application mints is a failure somewhere rather than a silently smaller set of unsubscribe requests; this step changes it for a reason that is stated, and the two unsubscribe cases that follow keep taking the first and second tokens of the list.
